item.title: [The Lancet] [Comment] Is chemotherapy still needed in all patients with mismatch repair-deficient advanced or recurrent endometrial cancer?
item.description: Around a quarter of advanced or recurrent endometrial carcinomas are mismatch repair deficient (dMMR).1 Addition of a PD-1 or PD-L1 inhibitor to carboplatin plus paclitaxel has transformed first-line treatment for this subgroup, with the RUBY,1 NRG-GY018,2 AtTEnd,3 and DUO-E4 trials reporting hazard ratios (HRs) for progression-free survival of 0·28–0·42 in their dMMR populations, and 4-year follow-up of RUBY suggests that some patients might be cured.5 However, every one of these trials retained chemotherapy.

item.title: [The Lancet] [Comment] The overlooked role of CMV in pneumonia in infants with HIV
item.description: For decades, severe pneumonia in infants with HIV has been treated as a race against time. Clinicians rapidly initiate broad-spectrum antibiotics, empirically treat suspected Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia, provide supportive care, and increasingly consider empirical tuberculosis treatment in high-burden settings, in line with WHO recommendations.1 Yet mortality remains unacceptably high despite these interventions.2 The EMPIRICAL trial by Cinta Moraleda and colleagues challenges another long-standing assumption; perhaps one important pathogen has been hiding in plain sight.

item.title: [The Lancet] [Comment] Empirical tuberculosis treatment in infants living with HIV: missed opportunities and ways to improve outcomes
item.description: Pneumonia remains the leading cause of death among infants living with HIV, with the case-fatality rate approaching 40%.1 Improving outcomes for these vulnerable infants demands new diagnostic and therapeutic approaches, yet current WHO guidelines for severe pneumonia in this population recommend only empirical coverage of Pneumocystis jirovecii and common bacterial respiratory pathogens.2 In addition, tuberculosis and cytomegalovirus are common causes of severe respiratory disease in infants living with HIV that remain unaddressed by current empirical therapy guidelines.

item.title: [The Lancet] [Comment] Offline: Anthony Fauci comes to London
item.description: “Shame on you”, screamed one protestor outside the Bloomsbury Theatre, London, UK. Anthony Fauci was to give the University College London Prize Lecture in Life and Medical Sciences. He has become a lightning rod for criticism among COVID-19 activists. Demonstrators were wearing sweatshirts emblazoned with “Refusenik” and “Covidiot”. Their banners told their story: “Killing our freedom only took one little prick”; “These vaccines are poison”; “The real Anthony Fauci: deadly pharma stooge”. When Fauci walked onto the stage inside the theatre, he received admiring applause.

item.title: [The Lancet] [Perspectives] Lalitha Regi and Regi George: strengthening community health
item.description: Working as doctors in a rural hospital in Tamil Nadu, India, married couple Lalitha Regi and Regi George realised that clinical care alone would not solve their patients’ health problems. The hospital “was a bottomless pit that you are just feeding and feeding. You send somebody back to their village, and they'll come back after 2 years with the same problem”, recalls Regi.

item.title: [The Lancet] [Perspectives] Critical thinking about assisted dying
item.description: Assisted dying has been a hot political issue in the UK. The Scottish Parliament voted against it in March, 2026. The Isle of Man's Assisted Dying Bill received Royal Assent in October, 2026, but there is no date yet for its implementation. And in the UK Parliament, the Terminally Ill Adults (End of Life) Bill, introduced by Kim Leadbeater MP in 2024, was defeated in the House of Commons in September, 2026. item.title: [The Lancet] [Perspectives] Silencing: a medical intern in the Gaza Strip
item.description: One of us (OA) completed his final year of medical school in the Gaza Strip. Omar lived in Khuza'a, a small farming village bordering Israel in south Gaza. His family are refugees from a village near Jaffa, now part of Tel Aviv in Israel. In the decades since their expulsion in 1948, all traces of this village have vanished. Despite being a refugee isolated from the wider world by the lengthy blockade of Gaza, Omar was a successful student, talented researcher, and leader of the student union.

item.title: [The Lancet] [Correspondence] The Perth Declaration to eliminate rheumatic fever and rheumatic heart disease
item.description: The persistence of rheumatic heart disease reveals how profoundly social inequity can shape who benefits from medical progress. Approximately 55 million people live with the disease, and more than 370 000 die each year.1 It is the most common acquired heart disease in people younger than 25 years, occurring during the years in which these individuals finish their education, form families, and build working lives. Rheumatic heart disease affects women and girls in greater numbers than men and boys,1 and their needs have too often been overlooked.

item.title: [The Lancet] [Correspondence] WHO's operational role in emergencies: a view from Gaza
item.description: Richard Brennan and colleagues make a timely case for maintaining WHO's operational capacity in emergencies.1 Amid severe financial constraints and wider reforms across the UN and the international humanitarian response system, WHO, like other international organisations, might need to become leaner and focus its constrained resources on its core mandate and areas of greatest comparative advantage.

item.title: [The Lancet] [Correspondence] Evidence and gaps for preventing postpartum haemorrhage
item.description: The claim by Ioannis D Gallos and colleagues that tranexamic acid does not have a preventive role does not reflect the scientific evidence.1 The Sustainable Development Goal is to reduce the maternal mortality ratio to fewer than 70 per 100 000 livebirths by 2030.2 Tranexamic acid is the only intervention shown to prevent death from bleeding in randomised trials.3,4 Early administration is most effective. Giving tranexamic acid to all women giving birth would reduce maternal deaths in countries where the risk of maternal death from bleeding is five or more per 100 000 births.

item.title: [The Lancet] [Correspondence] Evidence and gaps for preventing postpartum haemorrhage – Authors’ reply
item.description: We thank Judith Lieber and colleagues and Gabriele Saccone and colleagues for their responses to our Series. Lieber and colleagues’ comment highlights the importance of distinguishing evidence for prevention from evidence for treatment. We agree with them that tranexamic acid is a life-saving treatment for postpartum haemorrhage and should be given promptly after diagnosis. item.title: [The Lancet] [Articles] Empirical tuberculosis treatment in infants living with HIV hospitalised with severe pneumonia in Africa (EMPIRICAL): a multicentre, randomised, open-label, 2 × 2 factorial, controlled superiority trial
item.description: In contrast to empirical treatment with valganciclovir, there was no evidence that eTB-T was superior to a clinically and microbiologically guided strategy in reducing all-cause mortality among infants with HIV-associated pneumonia. However, the high proportion of infants who eventually initiated tuberculosis treatment during follow-up in the non-eTB-T groups might have reduced the contrast between strategies and attenuated the ability to detect differences in outcomes.
